newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy union, employers must sort out dispute - Prodi.
newsitem.headline: Italy union, employers must sort out dispute - Prodi.

text.p: The Italian government has played its part in mediating for metal workers' unions and employers in a bitter pay row and finding a solution is now up to the parties involved, Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Friday.
"The government has already taken an initiative a few weeks ago," Prodi told reporters in Rome. "Now it's up to the parties to go ahead and get to grips with the problem."
Italian Labour Minister Tiziano Treu has been mediating between the two sides in negotiations over the renewal of contracts for some 1.7 million workers.

Talks stalled last year and employers' federation Federmeccanica has since rejected government suggestions that workers should be given a 200,000 ($129) a month pay rise to cover the 1996-98 contract period.
Prodi's undersecretary Enrioco Micheli told reporters earlier that "The government has played its part, we cannot impose (a solution)."
Micheli said the government has been asked to restate an accord of July 1993, which is at the heart of the dispute.
"We have done so on several occasions. But we'll see, we are available. It would be a shame to spoil the possible beginnings of an economic recovery with social tension," he said.

The landmark 1993 accord scrapped automatic index-linked salary increases. Unions say the accord allows for full reimbursement for higher-than-expected inflation in the past contract period, but management disagrees.
Unions, which originally asked for 230,000 lire a month, have accepted the government's proposal but management has stuck to its 139,000 lire offer.
The deadlock prompted unions this week to call 10 hours of strikes until January 25, the third major strike called by the unions in the six-month dispute.

Separately, leaders of Italy's powerful CGIL, CSIL and UIL trades union confederations wrote to Prodi asking for a meeting of unions and employers association Confindustria to look at the July 1993 accord and the responsibilities of its signatories.
"We are sure that you too are worried like us about the climate of social tension which is growing, with the risk that it might extend beyond the confines of the metalworkers' contracts," they wrote.
"We are waiting to know what you propose on the basis of the requests we have put forward," they said.
